faq.a: Take a focused history, perform a chest exam, and obtain a rapid malaria test and chest X‑ray if possible.
faq.q: What is the first step when a patient presents with fever and cough in a low‑resource setting?

faq.a: Examine for peripheral oedema, elevated JVP and lung crackles (heart failure); check haemoglobin – severe anemia will have low Hb with a hyperdynamic pulse.
faq.q: How do I differentiate heart failure from severe anemia as a cause of dyspnoea?

faq.a: As soon as the diagnosis is confirmed, unless there is an acute opportunistic infection requiring immediate treatment first.
faq.q: When should I start antiretroviral therapy in a newly diagnosed HIV patient?

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer with fever, chills and a negative malaria test – what is your next diagnostic step? — Consider bacterial sepsis; obtain blood cultures and start empiric ceftriaxone.

A patient with known hypertension presents with sudden dyspnoea, crackles and an S3 gallop – which bedside sign distinguishes acute heart failure from pneumonia? — Presence of elevated JVP and peripheral oedema points to heart failure.
In a patient with HIV and a CD4 count <200, which prophylactic medication is essential and why? — Co‑trimoxazole to prevent Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia; it also covers some bacterial infections.

You have a febrile child with sickle‑cell disease and a negative blood film for malaria – what infection should you suspect first? — Consider bacterial sepsis, especially from Streptococcus pneumoniae; start broad‑spectrum antibiotics.

A patient on furosemide develops hyponatraemia – what is the likely mechanism and how would you manage it? — Loop diuretics cause renal sodium loss; replace with isotonic saline and adjust diuretic dose.
When is a bedside ultrasound preferred over a chest X‑ray in low‑resource settings? — When rapid assessment of pleural effusion or pericardial tamponade is needed and radiography is unavailable.
Why is quinine avoided in a patient with known QT prolongation? — Quinine can further prolong QT, increasing risk of torsades de pointes; use artemisinin‑based therapy instead.

A patient with chronic hepatitis B presents with mild transaminase elevation but normal bilirubin – what is the next step? — Assess viral load and liver fibrosis; start antiviral therapy if HBV DNA is high or fibrosis is advanced.
ai.title: Internal Medicine Overview
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A concise guide to thinking like an internist in low‑resource African hospitals. Covers diagnostic approach, common tropical causes, key investigations, red flags, management and exam strategies.

b: Diagnose by pattern recognition and systematic exclusion of different organ system pathologies
Use WHO/ICD‑10 coding for documentation when possible
sections.p: Internal medicine is the specialty that manages adult patients with complex, multisystem diseases, using history, physical exam and focused investigations.

b: Mild: stable vitals, no organ failure
Moderate: one organ dysfunction, requires monitoring
Severe: multiple organ failure, ICU referral
sections.p: Severity is judged by organ dysfunction, need for supportive care and prognostic scores (e.g., qSOFA for sepsis, NYHA for heart failure).

b: Infections: malaria, HIV‑related opportunistic infections, TB, bacterial sepsis
Cardiovascular: hypertension, rheumatic heart disease, heart failure
Metabolic: diabetes, sickle‑cell crises, chronic kidney disease
Hepatic: viral hepatitis B/C, schistosomiasis‑related fibrosis
sections.p: In East African settings the most frequent internal‑medicine presentations are infections, chronic non‑communicable diseases and complications of endemic conditions.

b: Ask about travel, animal exposure, herbal medicines
Identify red‑flag symptoms: chest pain, altered mental status, oliguria
sections.p: Patients often present with nonspecific symptoms—fever, weight loss, dyspnoea, abdominal pain—requiring a structured history and exam to narrow the differential.
Select tests that answer a specific clinical question; when a test is unavailable, use bedside alternatives.

t.b: Is there anaemia, leukocytosis or thrombocytopenia? Guides infection vs. marrow disease
Is malaria present? Positive test confirms Plasmodium infection; if unavailable, treat empirically in febrile patients with travel to endemic area
Is renal function impaired? Determines need for fluid adjustment and drug dosing
Is there pneumonia, heart failure or TB? Guides antibiotics vs. diuretics
Is there protein, blood or infection? Helps detect kidney disease or urinary sepsis
Is the patient HIV positive? Positive result changes infection work‑up and prophylaxis

b: Septic shock (SBP <90 mmHg, lactate >2 mmol/L)
Acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary oedema
Acute kidney injury with oliguria <0.5 mL/kg/h
Altered mental status or seizures
sections.p: Identify conditions that require urgent referral or intensive care.

b: Antibiotics: ceftriaxone for severe bacterial infection; avoid aminoglycosides in renal failure
Antimalarials: artemisinin‑based combination therapy; avoid quinine in cardiac arrhythmia
Antiretroviral therapy: start once HIV confirmed; avoid zidovudine in severe anaemia
Diuretics: furosemide for pulmonary oedema; monitor electrolytes
Insulin: basal‑bolus for uncontrolled diabetes; avoid sulfonylureas in renal impairment
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide organ‑supportive care. Choose drugs that are affordable, have a wide therapeutic index and are available locally.

b: Re‑check labs after 48‑72 h of treatment
Vaccinate against hepatitis B, pneumococcus and influenza
Promote insecticide‑treated nets and safe water
sections.p: Arrange regular review, health education and vaccination where possible.

b: Malaria vs. bacterial sepsis – both cause fever, but malaria has periodic chills and positive rapid test
Heart failure vs. COPD exacerbation – dyspnoea present in both; look for peripheral oedema and JVP in heart failure
sections.p: Conditions that mimic common internal‑medicine presentations.

b: Normal white cell count in severe malaria
Negative sputum smear in early TB – repeat or use GeneXpert if available
sections.p: Laboratory or bedside findings that may be falsely normal or abnormal.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe chest pain radiating to arm or jaw
Rapidly worsening shortness of breath with cyanosis
